title: Al-A'raf
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Al-A'raf is the seventh surah of the Qur'an. It has two hundred and six verses, it was revealed in Makkah, and it opens with the letters "Alif-Lãl-Mĩm-Ṣãd". Its name means "The Heights". The surah takes up two large subjects, the return to the Hereafter and the prophets who were sent, and it carries them in turn. First comes the reckoning and the arrogance that provokes it, with the story of Adam and Eve at the heart of that part. Then comes the long roll of messengers and the nations that answered them or refused them. At the end the surah turns back to the Book itself and to the Prophet ﷺ who was charged with carrying it.

There is a second way to describe what the surah is doing, and it is worth holding beside the first. The Book that comes down at its head is, in its essence, a book of guidance. But a book of guidance is worth little to anyone who has not kept his conscience alive. For everyone else it amounts to nothing more than a warning of the grievous fate they are moving towards because of their arrogance. The preacher of truth is troubled by what he sees. What is paramount in his eyes, the absolute truth, is rejected by the majority of the people as a falsehood, and treated with unconcern, as if it had no substance, as if it were completely unreal. The surah is written for that situation. It shows what the truth is, what the messengers carried, what happened to the nations that refused them, and where the account of the nations finally comes to rest.

### What its name means

- **Al-A'raf**, "The Heights". The surah takes the name up in its middle, in verses 46 to 49, where the Heights are described as a barrier between Paradise and the Fire, and the people who are stopped there are given a place of their own.
- The letters that open it, "Alif-Lãl-Mĩm-Ṣãd", are the same kind of opening found at the head of a number of other surahs. Their meaning is not settled, and the surah does not explain it.

### The two subjects of the surah

Looking across the whole of it, most of what the surah deals with falls under one of two headings. The first is ma'ad, the return to the Hereafter, and it runs from the opening of the surah up to about the end of the sixth of the surah's sections. The second is risala, prophethood, and from about the eighth section to the twenty-first the surah gives a detailed account of past prophets, of what happened to their communities, of the reward and the punishment they met, and of the punishment that overtook those who refused them.

The first stretch of the surah is therefore about the return itself and about the reckoning that goes with it. It begins with the Book and what it is for, tells people to follow what has been sent down to them and to take no protectors besides their Lord, and warns that many a community before them was destroyed while its people slept or were at their midday rest. It asks what answer the messengers and the peoples they were sent to will give on the Day of Resurrection, then sets out the weighing of deeds on that day and the pride of Iblis that put human beings under the power of the devil. The account of Adam and Eve and the garden closes that first movement, with the clothing Allah gave them and the promise of pardon.

### What the surah covers

The middle of the surah carries on in shorter movements. It shows how the righteous answer a messenger and how the arrogant refuse one, and it insists that the people who follow a bad leader share in the reckoning of that leader. It describes the reward of the believers and the punishment of the disbelievers, and it pictures the promise of Paradise and the threat of the Fire as two voices addressing the same people. Between them stands the Heights, and the disbelievers are shown begging the believers for a drop of water on the Day of Resurrection and being refused. The Book is then named for what it is, a source of knowledge, of guidance and of mercy, and the Creator is named with the beautiful names and with the command to call on Him. Two parables follow, the rain that brings the dead land back to life, and the field that yields or the field that does not.

Then the surah settles into the stories of the messengers, and this is the longest run in the book. Nuh (Noah) comes first, and his people call him a liar, accuse him of following only what he wants for himself, and are swept away by the flood. Hūd is sent to the people of 'Ad, who are destroyed by a wind. Ṣāliḥ (Salih) is sent to Thamud, who carve their houses out of the rock and are destroyed by an earthquake. Lūt (Lot) confronts a people whose wrongdoing is described plainly, and the angels come to him and to his family. Shu'aib is sent to Madyan with the demand that his people give the full measure and take what is due, and the leaders of Madyan threaten him, and the destruction that follows settles the matter. After these the surah steps back and names the pattern: nations are tested with ease and with hardship, and the end of one is the beginning of the next.

Mūsā (Moses) fills the next long stretch. His mission to Fir'awn, the contest with the magicians, the magicians' conversion and the threat that follows it, the plagues sent on Egypt, the golden calf, the appointment with Allah and the tablets, and the prayer of the one who was faithful all belong to this part. After him the final prophet is described and the message is declared for all of humankind. The surah then turns to the Israelites and their covenants, to the man who deviated from the straight path, to the statement that guidance comes from Allah alone, to the beautiful names and to the creation of human beings and the trap of ingratitude. It ends with the true guardian, the return of the soul to its Maker, the Prophet ﷺ and his noble character, the whisperings of the devil, and the last instruction to remember Allah and to be humble before Him.

### How it connects to the surah before it

Al-An'am, the surah that comes before this one, ends on the question of the earth and of what is entrusted to the people placed on it. Al-A'raf opens at a different height. Its first theme is not the world and its stewardship but the Book and the purpose of the Book, and everything after that first theme is arranged around the two questions the surah names for itself: what the Hereafter is, and what a messenger is for.

### In short

- Al-A'raf is the seventh surah, two hundred and six verses, revealed in Makkah, and it opens with the letters "Alif-Lãl-Mĩm-Ṣãd".
- It has two subjects, the return to the Hereafter and the prophets who were sent, and it devotes its longest stretch to the messengers and the fate of their communities.
- The Book is guidance for those who keep their consciences alive and a warning of the grievous fate for everyone else.
- Its middle holds the Heights, where the people who are stopped between Paradise and the Fire are described, and the disbelievers' final begging of the believers.
- It closes on the Book, the Prophet ﷺ and the instruction to remember Allah with humility.

1.text:
Al-A'raf opens with four letters that stand alone. The verse is nothing but "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd", and it is the first thing a reader meets in the surah. These are the disconnected letters, the same device that opens a number of other surahs, and the explanation of them was given once already, at the head of Al-Baqarah. Al-A'raf does not repeat that explanation and does not add to it. It sets the letters at the door and waits. What comes through the door is the Book itself, and the verse that follows speaks of nothing else.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd"** is the whole of the verse. These are isolated letters of the alphabet. They are not a word, and they carry no sentence. A number of other surahs open the same way, and in each case the letters stand alone before the first real statement of the surah begins.

### What the letters mean

Two answers are on record, and the surah leaves the question where it found it. One, reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, reads the letters as a way of naming Allah, saying of them: I am Allah who knows best and is best. The other takes them for an oath, a solemn pledge by which Allah swore. A third voice states the matter more plainly and says only that Allah knows best what He means by these letters.

The important point for a reader is that the question was dealt with before, at the head of Al-Baqarah, and that this surah refers back to it rather than starting the argument again. The letters are therefore an opening the reader has already learned to pass through. Their meaning is not needed to understand what follows, because the Book that comes next explains itself as it goes.

### In short

- The verse is four isolated letters, the disconnected letters that open a number of other surahs.
- Their explanation was given at the head of Al-Baqarah, and this surah does not repeat it.
- Two readings are on record: the letters name Allah, or they are an oath. Allah knows best what He means by them.

2.text:
The second verse explains what the letters were standing in front of. The Book has been sent down to the Prophet ﷺ, and he is told what to do with it and what not to worry about. "˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺—do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it—so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺, and as a reminder to the believers". Two audiences are named. There are the disbelievers, who are to be warned, and the believers, who are to be reminded. The command to the Prophet ﷺ is to carry the Book to both, and the one thing forbidden to him is anxiety about it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺"** points to the Qur'an. The words are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Book is the one that was revealed for him from his Lord and Master of everything. One gloss names the agent: this is the Scripture that Gabriel brought to you. Another has the whole clause read as a direct address, so that the words say to the Prophet ﷺ: this is a Book revealed to you. A further gloss ties "that you may warn" to the phrase "is revealed", so that the sentence reads, it is revealed for the purposes of warning.

**"do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it"** is the heart of the verse. The Arabic word behind it means constraint, or inhibition, or heaviness in the breast. Two quite different things can be meant by it, and both are on record. The first is doubt about the Book itself, that is, do not have any doubt in your heart that the Qur'an comes from Allah. Mujāhid, Qatādah and as-Suddī understood the words this way. The second is hesitation about carrying it, that is, do not hold back from conveying the Qur'an and warning with it, and do not let the fear of being called a liar weigh on you. Abū al-ʿĀliyah put the second sense this way: the Prophet ﷺ is to feel neither anguish nor apprehension about passing on the Qur'an and its instructions, in case people belie it and hurt him.

**"so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺"** gives the purpose of the sending. The Book came down so that the Prophet ﷺ could warn the disbelievers with it. The gloss that names the people and the place makes it more exact, and adds the aim: to warn the people of Makkah by means of the Qur'an, so that they may come to believe. Another reading says the Book was sent down in order to warn people by it and to be a proof.

**"and as a reminder to the believers"** gives the second purpose. The Book reminds those who have faith, and the point is added that they are the ones who benefit from being reminded. The two purposes are not rivals. Warning and reminding are what one Book does to two different kinds of hearer, and the verse says so in a single breath.

### Two ways to read "do not let anxiety into your heart"

The difference between the two readings is worth keeping, because the second one carries a further layer. On that reading the constraint in the breast is not the Prophet's own doubt but a real ache. It is the pain of a man who loves his people and is hurt by their refusal to believe even after hearing the Qur'an and its instructions. The verse does not deny that ache. It removes it from the Prophet's responsibility.

The link with the next of the Prophet's own attributes is made explicit elsewhere in the Qur'an, in the command to endure patiently as the messengers of firm resolve did (46:35). Patience there and freedom from anxiety here are two faces of the same instruction. The Book is not a weight to be carried alone. It is given to a messenger so that he can pass it on.

### Why he should not be anxious

The reassurance has a ground, and the ground is protection. Allah who sent this Book down has also arranged that the Prophet ﷺ will remain safe, and that arrangement takes care of any anguish on his part. The duty that was placed on him is a single duty: to make the call and to convey the message. And when that task is complete, the question of who accepts and who refuses is no longer his to answer. There was therefore no reason for him to be anxious about the outcome.

That is the whole answer to the verse, and it is a good one to sit with. A preacher is not the author of what he preaches and is not the judge of how it is received. The anxiety belongs to the one who is being warned, not to the one who carries the warning.

### In short

- The Book is the Qur'an, sent down to the Prophet ﷺ, and Gabriel is named as the one who brought it.
- "Do not let anxiety into your heart" can mean do not doubt the Book, and it can mean do not hesitate to convey it. On the second reading the anxiety is the Prophet's own pain at his people's refusal to believe.
- The verse names two audiences: the disbelievers are to be warned, the believers are to be reminded.
- The ground of the reassurance is protection. The duty is only to convey, and the result belongs to Allah.

3.text:
The command moves from what the Prophet ﷺ is to feel to what the hearers are to do. "Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him. How seldom are you mindful". The verse is addressed to the whole community that the Book came down to, and it asks two things of them. Take what has been sent down and follow it. Do not set up anyone else as a protector. The last clause is the verdict on how little of this the people will actually do.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord"** means follow and imitate the unlettered Prophet ﷺ, who brought you a Book revealed for you from the Lord and Master of everything. In practice the command has two sides. Uphold as lawful that which the Book makes lawful and unlawful that which it makes unlawful. And act on what the Messenger brought, obeying him in it and leaving everything else aside.

**"and do not take others as guardians besides Him"** means do not set up anyone else as a protector. The word used is the one for patrons or protectors, those whose authority is obeyed. Taking such people as lords means worshiping idols as lords. It also means obeying them in disobedience of Allah. And it means turning to the desires of those you imagine to be friends and protectors, among the devils or among evil scholars, and leaving what was revealed to you because of their desires. The harm of it is described exactly: the person who does this is deviating from Allah's judgment to the decision of someone else.

**"How seldom are you mindful"** translates a word that can be read in two ways. The original reading has the first letter assimilated into the second, so it can be read tadhakkarūn, those who take admonition, or yadhakkarūn, those who are admonished. There is also a variant reading, tadhkurūn, those who remember. The word mā in the phrase meaning little is held by some to be an addition, and its only work is to emphasise how small the number is.

### Who are the guardians people take besides Allah?

The verse does not name a particular group of opponents, and it does not need to. The thing it rules out is a whole way of living. A community that has received a Book from its Lord has been given the standard by which everything is judged. To set up other guardians is to go looking for a second authority, and the effect is always the same. The judgment of Allah is replaced by the decision of someone else, and the person who does this has not merely chosen a different opinion. He has handed the whole affair over to a man.

That is why the command is worded as a prohibition on guardians rather than as a prohibition on a belief. The wrong is not only in believing in a partner alongside Allah. It is in the daily act of letting another party decide for you, and then calling that a matter of loyalty.

### A world of trial

This is a world of trial. Every one of us here may take the truth or leave it, and clever words to justify the choice are never hard to find. But this position is only a temporary one. When the period of trial comes to an end it will be plain to everyone that the preacher's words rested on eternal truths, and that sheer bias and egotism on their part is what prevented them from perceiving the truth that lay at the heart of what he said. It will be clear then that the arguments they advanced to contradict him were a falsification of the facts and were never a form of reasoning in any real sense.

The verse's last clause, how seldom you are mindful, belongs at the end of that description. People are not short of words and they are not short of excuses. What they are short of is the memory that would change their conduct.

### The warning behind the warning

Three verses elsewhere in the Qur'an put the same point in the same register, and they are worth reading beside this one. And most people will not believe, no matter how keen you are (12:103). If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah's Way (6:116). And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him (12:106). Taken together they say that the majority is not a reliable guide, and that following the majority is a form of straying.

### In short

- Follow what has been sent down, which means to follow the Prophet ﷺ, to act on the Book, and to leave what is besides it.
- Take no other guardians. Obeying them in disobedience of Allah is what the verse rules out, and the result is exchanging Allah's judgment for a man's decision.
- The word for being mindful has more than one reading, and the reading that survives is the severe one: they hardly take admonition at all.
- This is a world of trial, and the arguments against the truth are not reasoning. They will be seen for what they are at the end.

4.text:
The surah leaves the Prophet's own heart and turns to whole societies. "˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed! Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday". The verse does not name a single people. It gives a figure, and the figure is left open, and then it gives the reason in one clause. These were towns that were destroyed because they defied the messengers and rejected them. The next verse supplies the only words they managed to say.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed!"** In the Arabic the word meaning how many stands in front of the verb, and the sentence says of a city that its inhabitants have been destroyed, that is, We have willed its destruction. The towns were destroyed for defying the messengers and rejecting them. That behaviour led them to earn disgrace in this life, and the disgrace of this life led them to disgrace in the Hereafter.

**"Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday"** means that the command and the vengeance of Allah came over them by night, or while they were taking a midday nap. Both of those times are periods of rest and leisure, of heedlessness and amusement. One gloss puts it more simply: they were destroyed, and the terror came upon them as a raid by night or by day.

### The example of earlier messengers

The charge against these towns is not unbelief in the abstract. They were destroyed for defying the messengers and rejecting them, and the same fate is described elsewhere for the same reason. Other messengers had already been ridiculed before you, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule (6:10). Many are the societies We have destroyed for persisting in wrongdoing, leaving them in total ruin. Many are also the abandoned wells and lofty palaces (22:45). Imagine how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their comfortable living. Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We alone were the Successor (28:58).

The last of these is the most desolate. The dwellings are still there. The people are not.

### Why the punishment caught them unaware

The verse is interested in the timing, because the timing is the point. The same question is asked in another place in this surah, and the answer given there is the same. Did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep? Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play (7:97-98).

A further passage asks whether those who devise evil plots feel secure, and lists the ways in which a punishment can arrive without warning (16:45-47). Do those who devise evil plots feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them? Or that the torment will not come upon them in ways they cannot comprehend? Or that He will not seize them while they go about their day, for then they will have no escape? Or that He will not destroy them gradually? The passage closes with a reminder that your Lord is truly Ever Gracious, Most Merciful (16:47). The mercy is not a softening of the warning. It is the reason the warning is given in time to turn back.

The two moments named in this verse, night and midday, are the moments of greatest ease. A punishment that arrives then finds people at their most unready, with their guard down and their attention elsewhere.

### "At night or at midday"

The phrase for the midday rest is a rest taken halfway through the day, and it does not always involve sleep. The point of the wording is that the coming was not confined to one hour. Sometimes it came upon a town by night and sometimes it came in the day, so that no moment of the day was safe and no one could take comfort from the hour in which it had not yet come.

The people of the towns were not given a warning they could use. They were destroyed while they were at rest, and the one thing that could have saved them, the Book and the messenger, was what they had refused.

### No one could help them

They could do nothing to avoid the punishment when it came, and the false gods they had been worshipping could do nothing to protect them from it. Their own helplessness and the helplessness of what they trusted are the same fact, seen from two sides.

### In short

- The verse counts no people and names no town. It says how many towns were destroyed for defying the messengers and rejecting them.
- Their disgrace in this life led to their disgrace in the Hereafter, and their dwellings were left behind as ruins.
- The punishment came at night or at midday, in the hours of rest and heedlessness, and sometimes by night and sometimes by day, so no hour was safe.
- When it came they could do nothing to avoid it, and the gods they trusted could do nothing for them.

5.text:
The cry of the destroyed towns is one cry, and it is short. "Their only cry—when overwhelmed by Our torment—was, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.”". The verse exists to be read together with the one before it. The towns were destroyed while they slept, and the only thing they said when the punishment came was a confession. They had no defence, no excuse and no plea. They said the one thing that was true.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Their only cry"** translates a word that carries the sense of words spoken in a single breath. A gloss renders it as plea, because a plea is what people make when they have nothing else. But the following words show that no plea was made. Their only cry, their only words, when the might of Allah came upon them, was to say it.

**"when overwhelmed by Our torment"** marks the moment. The word for the punishment is the same one used a verse earlier, and one gloss renders it as the terror that destroys. Whatever else the people of these towns were, they were idolaters, and the punishment that destroyed them was the punishment that came on them.

**"was, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.”"** is the confession itself. They admitted their sins and admitted that they deserved to be punished. Another gloss puts the point in fewer words: their only option, once the punishment was on them, was to own the wrong they had done, and the wrong was their disbelief in Allah.

### The admission is not a plea

There is a difference between the two things a person can say at the end. A plea asks for something. This does not. The towns said only that they were wrongdoers, which is a statement of fact, and the difference is the whole meaning of the verse. When the moment came there was no speech to be made, because no speech had been made before it.

The confession is also the thing they had never made while they lived. It is said of them that their only words at the end were the acknowledgment of their wrongdoing, which means the acknowledgment was not there before. A community that has spent its life refusing the messengers is left, in its final hour, with no vocabulary except the truth it refused to speak.

### The same cry elsewhere

The Qur'an gives the same cry in another place, and the placement there is telling. Imagine how many societies of wrongdoers We have destroyed, raising up other people after them (21:11). They kept repeating their cry until We mowed them down, leaving them lifeless (21:15). The word there is more than the word here. Here the towns confess. There they are named as a category, and the sentence closes the account on them with a single word about what remains.

### In short

- Their only words when the punishment came were a confession: we were wrongdoers.
- The words were an admission, not a plea. Nothing had been said before that would have been worth saying now.
- The confession was the acknowledgment of wrongdoing through disbelief, and it came only at the end.

6.text:
The question comes next, and it is the question the whole opening of the surah has been leading to. "We will surely question those who received messengers and We will question the messengers ˹themselves˺". Two parties are summoned, and they are summoned on the same day. The peoples who had a messenger sent to them will be asked what they did with the message. The messengers will be asked whether they carried it. The verse states a procedure, and the two questions it states are mirror images of one another.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We will surely question those who received messengers"** means the communities to which messengers were sent, and the question is about their response to the messengers and about how far they carried out what was conveyed to them. The same question is put in the same way in two other places. And watch for the Day He will call to them, asking, “What response did you give to the messengers?” (28:65). Consider the Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, “What response did you receive?” They will reply, “We have no knowledge compared to You! You alone are indeed the Knower of all unseen.” (5:109).

**"and We will question the messengers ˹themselves˺"** is the other half. The messengers are asked about the conveying of the message: did they hand over what they had been charged with, and how did their communities answer them? The reply of the messengers is given in the same passage, and it is the reply of creatures who have no knowledge of the unseen except what their Lord has told them.

### What the question is about

A reading of the verse reported from Ibn ʿAbbās says the questioning is about what the messengers conveyed. In other words the whole scene is about the message and the delivery of it. What the peoples did with it and what the messengers did in carrying it are two halves of one question, and the two parties stand on the same footing before it. The record that answers the question is described in the next verse, where Ibn ʿAbbās has the Book itself produced and made to speak.

### What the Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions about this

The Prophet ﷺ put the same question to his own Companions while he was still alive, in the address of his Last Hajj. He asked them what answer they would give on the Day of Resurrection, when they are questioned about him and about whether he carried Allah's message to them. Every Companion present answered that they would tell Allah that the message had reached them, that the trust of Allah had been fulfilled in the best way, and that the Prophet ﷺ had wished and done what was most beneficial for the community. The Prophet ﷺ then said: Allah, You be witness. The report is in Muslim, on the authority of Jābir.

In the Musnad of Aḥmad the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that on the Day of Resurrection Allah will ask him if he has conveyed His message to His servants, and that he will answer that he has. He added the instruction that follows from it: each of you must take care that the people who are there pass on what he has said to the people who are not there.

### The duty to pass the message on

Those absent covers two kinds of people. There are those who were alive at that time but were not present at that particular gathering, and there are the generations who come after. To convey the message to them means that people of every time should continue the chain of conveyance, each generation handing it to the next, so that every child of Adam born right through the Day of Resurrection will have received this message.

That is a heavy responsibility and a generous one. The question of verse 6 is asked of the messengers, and the answer given here is that the messengers do not stand alone in the duty of conveyance. It is passed on. And the verse in the opening of this surah about questioning the peoples who had messengers sent to them is answered, at least in part, by the community that keeps passing the message along.

### In short

- Two parties are questioned on the Day of Resurrection: the peoples who received messengers, and the messengers themselves.
- The peoples are asked what they did with the message. The messengers are asked whether they delivered it. The questioning is about what the messengers conveyed.
- The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions what they would say on that day, and they said that he had conveyed the message and fulfilled the trust, and he made Allah the witness.
- The duty of conveyance is not left to the messengers alone. Each generation must pass the message to those who come after it, so that all of humanity receives it.

7.text:
The last of the four verses brings the scene to its close. "Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—for We were never absent". After the question comes the record, and after the record comes the reason why the record is complete. The sentence is short and it settles everything. Nothing was missed, nothing was overlooked, and no one was absent when it happened.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then We will give them a full account"** means that they will be told the whole of their story, and that they will be informed with elucidation. The emphasis on the completeness of the account is deliberate. One gloss explains the account in this way: the Book is produced on the Day of Resurrection, and it speaks, telling out what its people used to do.

**"with sure knowledge"** marks the certainty of the telling. Nothing is reported at second hand and nothing is left to inference. What they did is known, and it is set before them plainly.

**"for We were never absent"** gives the ground of all of it. Allah was not absent when the messengers were conveying the message, and He was not absent during the time of the communities that came before and what they did. Another gloss puts the same point in plain terms: He was aware of everything they did, nothing of it was hidden from Him, and at no moment was He away from them.

### Nothing escapes His observation

The reason for the certainty is stated plainly in the verse that follows elsewhere in the Qur'an. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything, green or dry, but is written in a perfect Record (6:59). He witnesses to everything, and nothing escapes His observation. He is never unaware of anything. He knows perfectly what the eye is tricked into seeing and what the heart keeps hidden.

The point about the heart is the one to hold on to. A person may deceive everyone around him, and may even deceive himself, and the account that is given of him is still complete. The full account is not built from what was seen and reported. It is built from what is known.

### What the closing clause really says

The words "for We were never absent" do more than close a gap. They are the reason the account can be trusted. If there were absences, if there were moments when the watching stopped, then the record would be partial, and a partial record could be argued with. There are no such moments. The whole of what people did, in the small hours of their ordinary lives and in the decisions they thought nobody saw, was witnessed and was written down.

That is why the nations in the previous verses could not answer. They had no one to appeal to. The verdict had already been made, and it had been made by a witness who never left the room.

### In short

- After the questioning comes the full account, set out with certainty and without any gap in it.
- Ibn ʿAbbās read the account as the Book itself, brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, speaking and disclosing what they used to do.
- The ground of the certainty is that Allah was never absent, neither when the messengers were conveying the message nor during the times of the communities before them.
- Nothing escapes His observation, including what the eyes are deluded by and what the hearts conceal.

8.text:
The surah turns from the destroyed towns to the weighing itself. "The weighing on that Day will be just. As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺, ˹only˺ they will be successful". Two sentences, and between them a whole future is decided by the position of a balance. The verse also answers the obvious objection before it can be raised. Human deeds have no bulk and no mass, so how can they be weighed at all? The answer is that the weighing is fixed and certain, and the wording is deliberate so that nobody can afterwards claim they did not know.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The weighing on that Day will be just"** means that the weighing of deeds on the Day of Resurrection is the true weighing, and the reason given is that Allah will not wrong anyone. The wording is exact. Al-haqq, "the true", qualifies al-wazn, "the weighing", as an adjective does. The day in question is the Day of Resurrection, and the balance itself has been described in a report as one with a tongue and two palms like a pair of scales.

**"As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺"** means those whose good deeds outweigh their bad. They are the successful, the triumphant, the ones who escape the wrath and the torment of Allah.

**"˹only˺ they will be successful"** closes the matter. A gloss on the app's rendering is that the successful are those who have reached the goal and been saved from what they feared.

### The weighing will be exact, and no one will be wronged

The whole of the Qur'an's treatment of the weighing is built on one assurance. The scales of justice will be set up on the Day of Judgment, so that no soul will be wronged in the least, and even a deed of the weight of a mustard seed will be brought forth, and Allah is sufficient as a vigilant Reckoner (21:47). Allah never wrongs anyone, even by an atom's weight, and if a deed is good He multiplies it many times over and gives a great reward out of His grace (4:40). The same is said in Surah Al-Anbiyaʾ and in Surah Al-Qariʿah: whoever has a heavy scale will have a life of bliss, and whoever has a light scale will have the abyss for a home, and the abyss is a scorching fire (101:6-11).

Another passage gives the whole day in three verses. When the Trumpet sounds, all kinship between them is gone for that Day, and not one of them will even think of asking after another. Those whose scale is heavy are the successful, and those whose scale is light have doomed themselves and will stay in the Fire forever (23:101-103).

### What exactly is put on the scale

Three answers are given in the material, and all three are held together rather than fought over.

The first is the deeds themselves. Al-Baghawi reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the deeds will be placed on the balance even though they are not material objects, and that these deeds will be given a real weight on the Day of Resurrection. The second is the Book of Records in which the deeds are written. A report describes a man being brought forth with ninety-nine scrolls of errors and sins, each of them as long as the sight can reach, laid on one side of the balance. Then he is brought a card on which "La ilaha illallah" is written, and he will say to his Lord: what weight can this small card possibly have against all those scrolls? The answer is that he will not be wronged, and the card is placed in the other pan. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of it: the ninety-nine scrolls will rise and the card will sink. A wording close to this is recorded by at-Tirmidhī, who calls it authentic.

The third is the person who did the deeds. A report says that a man will be brought forth whose weight in the sight of Allah is no heavier than the wing of a mosquito, and the verse that goes with it is that "on the Day of Resurrection We will not give their deeds any weight" (18:105). The Prophet ﷺ also spoke of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd in this way: his legs look so thin, yet by Him in Whose Hand is my soul they will weigh more on the Balance than the mountain of Uhud.

The three can be reconciled without strain. Sometimes the deeds are weighed, sometimes the scrolls in which they are written, and sometimes the one who did them. Allah knows best.

### What the good deeds will look like when they arrive

Two further reports describe the deeds as things that can be seen and met. It is recorded in the Sahih that Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān will come on the Day of Resurrection as two dense clouds that cast their shade over those who recited them, or as two objects that give shade, or as two lined groups of birds. The Qur'an comes to the one who recited and kept it as a pale-faced young man. He will ask, "Who are you?" and the reply is, "I am the Qur'an, who made you stay up sleeplessly at night and caused you thirst in the day."

The report of al-Baraʾ about the questioning in the grave goes the same way for the good deeds. A young man with fair colour and a good scent will come to the believer, who will ask, "Who are you?" and he will reply, "I am your good deeds." The Prophet ﷺ described the reverse for the disbeliever and the hypocrite.

### How deeds that have no weight can be weighed

The objection is a sensible one, and it is met directly. Do not be deceived by the idea that things which are normally weighed or measured have some heaviness to them. Human deeds, good or bad, have no body and no mass. So how could they be weighed? The first answer is authority. The power of Allah is absolute, and there is nothing that He cannot do. Why should it be impossible for Him to weigh or measure human deeds, with or without a device?

The second answer is that the Creator can give a deed a material presence. People find it easier to believe in a film than in the religious account of what will come to pass, yet the Creator of the universe is in fact able to bring things into a shape at some point. There are many reports confirming that human deeds take particular shapes and forms during the barzakh, the state between death and resurrection, and on the plains of the Resurrection. Good deeds, in forms made fair, become the companions of the grave, and evil deeds crawl about in the shape of snakes and scorpions. One report says that a person who has not paid the zakah due on his wealth will have that wealth come to his grave as a venomous serpent, which bites him and tells him: I am your wealth, I am your treasure.

The third answer is that people have always been able to measure what cannot be weighed in the ordinary way. There are instruments now that weigh air, electric current, heat and cold, and a meter is all that is needed. If the Maker of makers can weigh or measure human deeds, what is there in that to call far-fetched?

There are verses for it. The record of deeds will be laid open, and the wicked will be seen in fear of what is written in it (18:49). In Surah Az-Zalzalah it is said that whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see that too. What matters is that the deeds of every person will be there on the plain of the Resurrection in a form that is perceptible.

### The wording was chosen on purpose

Because human beings judge everything by analogy from the conditions of their own life in this world, they reason about the Hereafter from what they can see and touch. That is the state the Qur'an describes in Surah Ar-Rum: they only know the worldly affairs of this life, but are totally oblivious to the Hereafter (30:7). They will shake the earth and the skies to find out what cannot be found, while the great field of reality that has to unfold in the life to come is something they are entirely unaware of.

So the verse says, in this exact form, that the weighing on that day is definite. The point of the careful wording is that a person caught up in the obvious and the perceptible may not afterwards be able to deny the weighing of deeds in the life to come, which is proved from the Qur'an and is the collective belief of the Muslim Ummah.

### The weighing is done twice

One set of scholars holds that the weighing on the plains of the Resurrection happens twice. First, belief and disbelief are weighed, and that is the weighing by which a believer is separated from a disbeliever. Whoever has even the declaration of faith written in the Book of Deeds has that scale become heavier, and he is set apart from the group of the disbelievers. Then comes a second weighing, of good deeds against bad deeds. In it the good deeds of one believer are heavy on the scale while the scale of another is heavy with evil, and each receives the punishment or the reward that follows from it. Once this is understood, the verses and the reports about the weighing are all in step with one another.

The reports that seem to pull the other way are the ones about the declaration of faith. At-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim all record from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that a man of the community will be brought before the whole of creation on the plain of the Resurrection, and ninety-nine Books of Deeds will be brought in, each scroll as long as the sight can reach, every one of them full of sins and evils. He is asked whether everything written there is correct, and he admits that it is, and in his heart he is nervous, wondering how he will find his deliverance. Then Allah says: today there is no injustice for anyone, and against all his sins there is set a testimonial of his being good, written where the declaration of faith is: "I testify that there is no god but Allah and I testify that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger." The man asks what weight this small note can carry against such a large black Book of Deeds, and he is told that no injustice will be done to him. The pan holding the note then becomes the heavier, and the pan full of sins tips up. After relating this the Prophet ﷺ said: nothing can weigh more than the name of Allah.

From the Musnad of al-Bazzār and the Mustadrak of al-Ḥākim, also from Ibn ʿUmar: at the time of his death Nūḥ (Noah) said "La ilaha illallah", because if the heavens and the earth were placed in one pan and the declaration of faith in the other, the pan containing the declaration would invariably remain the heavier. Narrations to the same effect come from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū ad-Dardāʾ, carried by reliable transmitters and spread across many collections of reports.

Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported in the collection on faith by al-Bayhaqī, put the two together: a believer whose good deeds outweigh on the scale goes to Paradise carrying his deeds with him, and the one whose evil deeds are heavier is sent to Hell with his deeds. A believing Muslim who recites the declaration of faith therefore finds the scale heavier in his favour, however many sins he carries.

But many verses and many reports also prove that good and bad deeds are weighed, so that for one the pan of good deeds is heavier and for another the pan of sins. And there is a further report from Abū Hurayrah in Abū Dāwūd: if a shortage is found in the obligatory duties of a servant, Allah will ask whether he has any voluntary acts to his credit, and if they are there the shortage of the obligatory is made up by the voluntary.

### What weighs heavy

There are reports that single out particular deeds because of how much they weigh.

One, narrated by Abū Hurayrah and appearing in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, says that on the Day of Resurrection some people will be brought forward who are heavy in appearance, yet in the sight of Allah they are worth no more than a mosquito's wing, and it is supported by the verse that on the Day of Resurrection no weight will be assigned to those who reject the signs of their Lord (18:105).

One of the virtues of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd is a report that his legs look so thin, yet on the balance of justice for the Day of Resurrection their weight is more than the weight of Mount Uhud.

There is the report of Abū Hurayrah with which al-Bukhārī closed his collection, in which two words are said to be very light when spoken and very heavy when weighed, and dear to Allah: Subḥānallāhi wa biḥamdihī, and Subḥānallāhi al-ʿaẓīm. From ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to say that saying Subḥān Allah fills half the pan, and that saying al-ḥamdu lillāh fills the other pan.

The three of them, Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥibbān, report on sound authority from Abū ad-Dardāʾ that no deed will be heavier than good character on the scale. To Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī the Prophet ﷺ said: I tell you of two things that are not difficult for anyone, yet on the scale of deeds they will be the heaviest. Good character, and keeping to silence, that is, not talking unless it is necessary.

In his book on asceticism Aḥmad reports from Ḥāzim that the angel Jibraʿīl al-Amīn came to the Prophet ﷺ while someone there was weeping from the fear of Allah. Jibraʿīl said: all human deeds will be weighed, but the tears that flow from the fear of Allah and the Hereafter are a deed that is not weighed. A single such tear would hold back the fiercest fire of Hell.

From Ibn al-Mubarak comes the account of a man on the plain of the Resurrection who looks at his Book of Deeds and sees very few good deeds there, and is nervous. Suddenly something rises like a cloud and falls into the pan of his good deeds, and he is told that the reason is the teaching of the faith, which went on multiplying as people acted on it, with a share set aside for him for every single follower of his teaching.

Aṭ-Ṭabarānī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that a person who goes to the graveyard with the funeral will have two karats placed on his scale, and other narrations give the weight of that karat as equal to Mount Uhud. He reports from Jābir that the first deed to be set on the scale is the good deed of providing for his family and looking after what they need. Al-Dhahabī reports from ʿImrān ibn Ḥusayn that on the Day of Resurrection the ink used by the scholars to set down the religion and its rulings will be weighed against the blood of the martyrs, and the ink will turn out to be the heavier.

### How the weighing is put in practice

One authority has said that the weighing may be repeated several times in different ways, and that the full reality of these matters is known to Allah alone. For a person going about his ordinary life, it is not necessary to know that reality. It is quite enough to know that the deeds will be weighed. If they turn out to be light, punishment is what is deserved, and then it is a separate matter whether Allah forgives in His grace, by Himself, or through the intercession of a prophet or a saint, and the person stands delivered. The claim that some people are saved solely because they said and believed the declaration of faith, and that all their sins are forgiven on that account, belongs to the exception, and is a special gift of the grace and mercy of Allah.

### The inner reading

Deeds weighed on the scale of self-purification, and states weighed on the scale of truthfulness. Wretched is the man whose deeds are stained by showing off and whose states are mingled with self-admiration, for at the station of the scales such states are worth nothing and such deeds have no weight. The verse is quoted to say that "on the Day of Resurrection We will not give their deeds any weight" (18:105).

Among the traditions of ʿUmar is this: "Take an accounting of yourselves before you are brought to account, weigh your deeds before they are weighed, and prepare for the Greatest Exposure." The sense of it is that you should take your own inventory and look at what you have actually done, and then ask yourself what you have stored up for the Greatest Exposure and for the day of the gathering. That is why the Lord of the Worlds said, "be mindful of Allah and let every soul look to what deeds it has sent forth for tomorrow, and fear Allah, for certainly Allah is All-Aware of what you do" (59:18).

It is reported that a man of intelligence has four hours set aside for seeking felicity and adorning his life. The first is the hour in which he takes an account of himself and weighs his own deeds and states. The second is the hour of private conversation with the Real, when he lays his need before Him. The third is the hour in which he takes care of his own livelihood. The fourth is the hour of rest in quiet prayer and in whatever this world has given him.

Those who walk the Tariqah and the lords of recognition hold that the scales are many. There is a scale for the soul and the spirit, a scale for the heart and the intellect, and a scale for recognition and the secret core. The first measures commands against prohibitions, and the two pans that meet are the Book and the Sunnah. The second measures reward, and its two pans are the threat and the promise. The third measures approval, and its two pans are fleeing and seeking. Fleeing means escaping this world to cling to the world to come. Seeking means leaving the world to come aside to look for the Patron.

### In short

- The weighing is the true weighing, because Allah wrongs no one. Not a mustard seed, not an atom, is overlooked.
- Three things are described as being weighed: the deeds, the scrolls in which they are written, and the person who did them. All three are held together, and Allah knows best.
- Deeds have no mass, and the answer is that the power of Allah is absolute, that He can give deeds a material presence, and that the record of deeds will be laid open.
- The declaration of faith outweighs any quantity of sins, so the weighing is done twice: once for belief, once for deeds.
- Nothing is what it seems in weight. Good character, silence, tears of fear, teaching the faith, a funeral, and spending on one's family all weigh more than their size suggests.

9.text:
The other half of the pair. The previous verse described the scale that sinks down. This one describes the scale that tips up, and it says what is on it and what the loss actually amounts to. "But those whose scale is light, they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs". The loss is self-inflicted. Nobody is taken away from Paradise, and nobody fails to arrive. They weigh themselves down, and the verse says so in the plainest terms.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those whose scale is light"** means those whose bad deeds outweigh their good ones. The reason is given in the same clause: they are light because of the evil they did.

**"they have doomed themselves"** means they have lost their own souls, and the loss is a punishment. One gloss puts it as the soul travelling towards the Fire. Another says that they gained their destruction on the Day of Judgment and were cut off from the eternal bliss, and the word for "doomed" in the Arabic carries the sense of destroying oneself. The parallel passage in the Qur'an says the same in a single line: those whose scale is light have doomed themselves and will stay in the Fire forever (23:103).

**"for wrongfully denying Our signs"** gives the cause and the aggravating circumstance. They knew. They denied the signs knowingly, and they denied them wrongfully, and the denial that condemned them was of the revelations of Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an.

### Where the light scale leads

The account of the light scale in Surah Al-Qariʿah is short and terrible. "And as for those whose scale is light, their home will be the abyss" (101:8-9). The word behind "abyss" is the pit, and the gloss given for it is Hell itself, and the question that follows has no comfortable answer: "And what will make you realize what that is? It is a scorching Fire" (101:10-11).

Two things are being said at once. The home is already settled, and the home is the Fire. And the verdict cannot be reopened, because the scale is not weighed twice. The parallel passage at 23:103 puts the outcome in the plainest possible words, and it is worth noticing what it does not say. It does not say that the fire will be lifted, or that the light scale will be weighed again, or that a late good deed might turn it. Those whose scale is light stay in the Fire forever.

The loss is also described as exclusion rather than merely as suffering. Those who are cut off from the bliss, cut off from it, and the cutting off is the punishment.

### The knowing that made it worse

The final clause is what turns the verse from a warning into an indictment. The denial was not a mistake, and it was not a failure to understand. It was a denial of signs that had been shown to them, and one gloss puts it as their mistreating of what they had already been given.

The signs they denied are named in another reading as the revelations of Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an itself. So nothing about the scale was hidden from them. They knew what the signs were, they knew what they were saying about them, and they said it anyway. A person who has seen a thing and then set it aside has not been short of information. He has been short of something else.

### What it means to lose yourself

The phrase is stronger than it looks. To lose yourself here is not to be disappointed, and not to fail in some hope. It is to be the cause of your own ruin, so that the losing is done by you and not done to you. A person is left with nothing, and what is left is the loss of the self, which is the one thing that cannot be replaced.

That is why the verse pairs the light scale with the deliberate refusal. The verse before it promised success to those whose scale was heavy. This one closes the other door. The scale does not tip by accident, and it is not tipped by an outside power. It tips because of what was put on it.

### The weight changes hands at the last day

In this world the importance of a person is judged by the material splendour around him and by his ability to move people with impressive words, and so to have a large following. The preacher of truth is generally not in that happy position. What he says carries no weight with the people of the world, while the words of his rivals, who are decked in worldly splendour, carry a great deal.

But when the Day of Judgment uncovers all the facts, the position is exactly reversed. All the weight then lies on the side of the truth. Untruth is stripped of all its arguments and rendered valueless, and the things that were counted for nothing are the things that carry the day.

That reversal is the point of the two verses together. The scale in verse 8 and the scale in verse 9 are the same scale, and the difference between the two kinds of people is not the scale but what was put on it. The world measures the wrong things. The Last Day measures the right ones.

### In short

- A light scale means the bad deeds outweigh the good, and the cause given is the knowing and wrongful denial of the signs.
- To doom yourself is the strongest phrase available: the ruin is self-inflicted, and the loss is of the self itself.
- The outcome is the abyss as a home and the Fire forever, and the same word is used in the parallel passage at 23:103.
- The world measures the wrong things, and the Last Day reverses every weighing.

10.text:
The surah turns again, from the weighing to the reason for hope. "We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks". After the warning comes the favour, and after the favour comes a complaint. The two verses before this one told a people what they had done to themselves. This one tells them what has been done for them, and then asks why they are not grateful for it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have indeed established you on earth"** is addressed to the children of Adam. The earth was made a fixed place for dwelling, with firm mountains and rivers set upon it, and homes, and its benefits put at the disposal of the people on it. The clouds were made to work for them, bringing rain, so that they might produce their sustenance from them.

**"and provided you with a means of livelihood"** points to the ways and means of earning, to trade and commerce, and to all the other trades and professions. A gloss spells out what the livelihood is for: a livelihood from which you eat, drink and clothe yourselves. The word is the plural of a word meaning the means by which a person is able to subsist.

**"˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks"** is the complaint. The word for "little" carries an extra particle that does nothing but emphasise how small the amount is. A gloss gives the sense in both directions: your thanks are small for everything that has been done for you, and you give no thanks at all, for the great things or for the small ones.

### Everything needed has been put in the earth

The earth is described as a storehouse. The Master of the Universe has made the whole of it, and everything in it, a vast warehouse of human needs and comforts, filled with a complete list of what people require. What is left for human beings is to go in, take out what they need and use it. Science and technology are a trained method of taking out what the Master of the Universe has stored there and using it soundly. One who has neither the sense nor the manners to reach into that storehouse, and who then fails to make proper use of what he took out, goes on deprived of the benefit. An intelligent person benefits from both.

The demand that follows is plain. Everything people need has been put into the earth by Allah, and that is a standing demand on them to be grateful to Him at every moment and in every circumstance. Human beings are prone to heedlessness, and they do not take long to forget the favours of their Creator and Master. That is why the verse ends in a complaint: you are so little receptive to advice.

### The reason the thanks are withheld

Whatever has been bestowed on human beings in this world was given to draw out their gratitude, and gratitude is the one thing they do not offer to their Lord. The reason is that the devil distorts their feelings and steers them away from every expression of gratitude.

The story of Adam and the devil shows the real criterion of a person's case. Human beings are judged at the point where jealousy and pride form in the heart. In this testing world the same situation keeps arising, in which one person ends up above another. Sometimes one person receives a greater share of wealth and honour than his fellow men. Sometimes, in a deal between two people, one of them treats the discharge of the other's legitimate rights as degrading to himself. On every such occasion a person is judged, and the question is whether he responds positively or reacts negatively. The pride that turns even a fair transaction into a wound is what blocks the response.

### The verse in the Qur'an's own summary

The same point is made in another verse: "He has granted you all that you asked Him for, and if you tried to count Allah's blessings you would never be able to number them. Indeed humankind is truly unfair and totally ungrateful" (14:34).

### In short

- The earth was made a place of dwelling, with mountains, rivers, homes and every trade and profession.
- The favour is universal and the requirement is gratitude at all times and in all conditions.
- Human beings forget quickly. The verse ends in a complaint, not in a blessing: you are so little receptive to advice.
- Gratitude is withheld because the feelings are distorted, and judgement falls where jealousy and pride begin.

11.text:
The third movement of the opening stretch, and the one that leads into the story of the garden. "Surely We created you, then shaped you, then said to the angels, "Prostrate before Adam," so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others". The verse turns from the human being to his origin and to the first refusal ever made against his Maker. Everything the rest of the surah will say about the devil and about the children of Adam starts here.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely We created you"** is the creation of Adam, and Adam is from dust. A gloss spells out the sense of what was given: the father of the human race was made in the best of forms and the best of designs. The verse addresses the whole of humanity through its first member, since the blessing of the father passes to the descendants.

**"then shaped you"** covers the second stage. Adam was shaped, and then his descendants were shaped in the wombs. A further gloss has Adam himself fashioned between Makkah and Ṭā'if.

**"then said to the angels, "Prostrate before Adam,""** records the command. The prostration was a bow of salutation, a greeting, and it was given to the angels who were on the earth. The order came after the shaping, because the command was given only once the human being was complete and the breath of life had been breathed into him.

**"so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others"** records the refusal. Iblīs was the leader of the jinn and was among the angels, and he was not of those who made prostration. He refused out of pride and stubbornness. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned the opposite case for the disbeliever and the hypocrite: the good deeds of the believer come to him in the grave as a young man with a fair complexion and a good scent.

### Why the verse speaks of one man in the plural

The verse refers to Adam although the word used is the plural, because Adam is the father of all mankind, and the honour and the enmity belong to him and are inherited by his children.

The same pattern is found in the Qur'an elsewhere, and the reason is the same. "And remember when We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails" (2:57). That was addressed to the Children of Israel, and it refers to their forefathers who lived in the time of Mūsā (Moses). Since the favour was given to the forefathers, and they are the very source of the offspring, the offspring have been favoured by it as well.

There is one verse that does not follow this rule. "And indeed, We created humankind from an extract of clay" (23:12). The sense there is only that Adam was made of clay. His descendants were made from the nutfah, the mixed discharge, and that verse speaks of where humankind came from in general, not saying that every human being was created from clay. Allah knows best.

### The honour and the enmity

Allah is informing the children of Adam of the honour of their father and of the enmity of the devil, who still carries jealousy towards them and towards their father Adam. They should therefore beware of him and not follow in his footsteps.

The scene is described more fully elsewhere. "When your Lord said to the angels, I am going to create a human being from sounding clay moulded from black mud" (15:28), and "So when I have fashioned him and had a spirit of My own creation breathed into him, fall down in prostration to him" (15:29). Once Allah had made Adam out of dried clay of altered mud and shaped him into a human form, and had breathed the soul into him, He gave the angels the order to prostrate to him, in honour of Allah's glory and His majesty. The angels all heard, obeyed and prostrated. Iblīs did not prostrate, and the story was told at the beginning of Surah Al-Baqarah.

### The inner reading

The wise Lord, the renowned and tremendous One who compels all, the knower of His servants, is reminding the children of Adam of His favours and teaching them about His goodness and His holding to the covenant. He is saying: I made you, and I shaped the beauty of your faces. I set your heights, and gave you two eyes that see, two ears that hear and a tongue that speaks. I am the Lord who brings being out of nothing, who produces what was not there, and who renews things from the very beginning.

It is I who paint the faces. It is I who adorn the beauties. It is I who pair each thing with its counterpart. It is I who make every being in a fitting way. It is I who made the heavens, the earth and the lifeless things, to show forth power. It is I who made the angels, the satans and the jinn, to show forth awe. It is I who made Adam and the Adamites, to show forth forgiveness and mercy. And for 700,000 years the one called Gabriel, and Michael, and Seraphiel, and the Cherubim, and the Circlers, and the Row-keepers made their circuits round the Kaʿbah of the One who compels all, crying "The Glorified, the Holy". They never gained access to the names of love, of loving kindness and of friendship, and they never had the presumption to claim friendship with Me. I, on the other hand, chose friendship with the people of dust. "We are your friends" (41:31). "He loves them" (5:54). Out of that friendship and that kindness towards them I took several of My names: the Forgiving, the Loving, the Clement, the Ever-Merciful. As for the angels, I showed them nothing but severity and the power that compels all, and I kept them behind the veils of awe. To the people of dust I showed nothing but gentleness and mercy, and I kept them on the carpet of bounty and expansiveness.

Among the angels, Gabriel was honoured and foremost, and he was singled out for the special favours of proximity. His name was the servant of the All-Merciful. He stood constantly on the carpet of justice with the attribute of awe, and he had never seen the carpet of bounty and expansiveness. Before Adam the chosen one came, there was no separation and no union, no rejection and no acceptance, and no talk of heart, of sweetheart and of friendship. All of these wonders and storehouses belong to the register of passion.

### In short

- The verse is about Adam, and it uses the plural because Adam is the father of all mankind. The honour and the enmity are his and are inherited by his children.
- "We created you" is Adam, who is from dust. "Then shaped you" covers the wombs, and the command to the angels came only after he was complete.
- The prostration was a greeting. Every angel obeyed. Iblīs, the leader of the jinn who was among the angels, refused out of pride and stubbornness.
- The parallel with 2:57 shows the same rule for the Children of Israel, and 23:12 is the one verse that does not follow it, since Adam's children are made from the nutfah.
